title: Breaking Changes
description: Identify, classify, and handle breaking API changes including removed fields, renamed endpoints, and changed semantics.

data.text: A breaking change is any modification to an API contract that causes existing clients to fail. Not all changes are obvious: adding a required field, changing a field type, or tightening validation can all break clients silently.

rows: Clients reading fullName get 404 or null
Change price from string to integer
JSON parse fails or wrong precision
Clients switch on old enum get 400
Require email format on previously free-form field

data.title: Breaking change: changing field type from string to object
data.content: A seemingly minor refactor can break every client. Use consumer-driven contract testing to catch these before production.

items: Add new fields as nullable or with defaults — never make them required in the same version
Deprecate fields before removing them: mark deprecated=true, return data for 12 months, then remove
Add new API versions for breaking changes instead of modifying existing endpoints
Use union types in strongly typed languages: return OldType | NewType during migration
Document breaking changes in a changelog with migration guides

data.title: The additive-only rule
data.text: If you must modify an existing contract without versioning, the only safe operations are: adding optional fields, adding new enum values, and widening accepted ranges. Everything else requires a new version or a deprecation cycle.

data.title: Pact consumer test catching a breaking change
data.content: Consumer-driven contract tests verify that the provider still satisfies the consumer's expectations before deployment.

items.question: How do I handle breaking changes in a public API?
items.answer: Never make breaking changes without a new version. Publish a deprecation notice 12 months in advance. Return 409 Conflict if a client uses a deprecated field and provide a migration path.

items.question: What if a breaking change is urgent (security patch)?
items.answer: Security fixes are an exception. Communicate the urgency clearly, provide a hotfix version, and offer extended support for the previous version. Document the CVE and timeline.

items.question: How do I communicate breaking changes to third-party developers?
items.answer: Use a changelog, email notifications, webhook events, and in-API response headers (Sunset, Deprecation). Provide a migration guide with code examples for every breaking change.

data.title: Key takeaway
points: Breaking changes require a new version or a deprecation cycle.
Contract tests catch breaking changes before they reach production.
Deprecate before remove: mark, monitor, then delete.
Security fixes are the only acceptable emergency breaking change.
data.takeaway: Treat your API contract like a public interface. Change it with the same care you would give a published SDK. If consumers depend on it, breaking it is a product decision, not just a technical one.
